title: The Pledge, the Ant, and Seven Things the LORD Hates
summary: The father warns his son to free himself quickly from a rash pledge made for someone else's debt, urges the lazy to learn from the ant, and describes the worthless man who stirs up trouble with twisted speech and gestures. A numerical saying lists seven things the LORD hates. The chapter closes with another warning against adultery, which, unlike theft driven by hunger, brings disgrace and a jealous husband's fury that no payment can settle.
story: Proverbs 6 interrupts the extended warnings about the forbidden woman (chapters 5 to 7) with a set of shorter teachings on money, work, and speech, before returning to adultery in verse 20. The variety matters: wisdom in this book reaches into business deals and sleep habits as well as sexual morality and worship. The list of what the LORD hates shows that the practical and the spiritual aren't separate categories; lying, arrogance, and stirring up division are offenses against God, not just social mistakes.
historical:
The chapter assumes an economy of loans, pledges, and debts, which Israel's law regulated. The law forbade charging interest to fellow Israelites who were poor (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37) and limited what a lender could take as a pledge, for example requiring a poor man's cloak to be returned by nightfall (Deuteronomy 24:12-13). Putting up security meant guaranteeing someone else's loan, so that if the borrower defaulted, the guarantor had to pay, sometimes with his land, his goods, or even his freedom.

The law of theft in Exodus 22:1-4 required a thief to repay double, or four or fivefold for livestock he had killed or sold. The sevenfold of verse 31 is probably not a legal figure but a way of saying full repayment, seven being a number of completeness. The contrast in verses 30 to 35 is that a thief, however guilty, can make restitution, while an adulterer faces a husband's anger that no compensation will satisfy.
cultural:
Striking hands (verse 1) was the gesture that sealed a pledge, the ancient equivalent of signing a contract. Once done, it bound a person in the eyes of the community. The father's urgent advice is to humble yourself and keep pressing the neighbor until you are released, like a gazelle or a bird breaking free from a hunter's trap. Sleep lost now is better than ruin later.

The ant was a familiar sight in the fields of the land of Israel, where harvester ants gather seeds and store them in underground chambers during summer and harvest. The father points out that the ant has no commander or overseer; it works without being forced. The worthless man of verses 12 to 15 communicates by winking, shuffling his feet, and pointing his fingers, signals of secret mockery or conspiracy in a culture where gestures carried a lot of meaning. His whole body is enlisted in deceit.
literary: The chapter is a collection of distinct units. Verses 1 to 5 address suretyship, verses 6 to 11 the sluggard, and verses 12 to 15 the troublemaker, each in the form of a short instruction or portrait. Verses 16 to 19 are a numerical saying, a form found elsewhere in Proverbs and in the prophets (Amos 1 and 2), in which the pattern six things, yes seven builds to a climax. The list moves down the body, eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet, and ends with the false witness and the one who stirs up discord, which is the climax and ties back to the troublemaker of verse 14. Verses 20 to 35 return to the father's voice and the adulteress, using rhetorical questions (can a man embrace fire and not be burned?) and a comparison with theft.

outline.t: Get free from a rash pledge
Go to the ant, you sluggard
The worthless man and his sudden ruin
Six things the LORD hates, seven he detests
The lamp of instruction and the fire of adultery

doctrines.note: The seven things the LORD hates are mostly sins of pride, speech, and relationships: haughty eyes, lying, violence, scheming, eagerness for evil, false testimony, and sowing discord. God's hatred of these shows how seriously he takes the damage they do to his people.
Verse 23 calls the father's commandment a lamp and his teaching a light, language that echoes Psalm 119:105. Wise instruction, rooted in God's law, lights the way through ordinary life.
Wisdom includes financial prudence and diligent work. The chapter treats reckless pledges and laziness as moral and spiritual failures, not only practical mistakes.

words.note: Arav, to pledge or stand surety. It means to guarantee someone else's debt, taking on their obligation, so that one person's debt becomes another's. Proverbs warns repeatedly against doing this rashly (11:15; 17:18; 22:26-27), especially for a stranger.

Atsel, sluggard or slacker. This is one of the book's stock characters, a comic and tragic figure who always has one more excuse to stay in bed. His poverty doesn't come from bad luck in these verses but from the slow accumulation of a little sleep, a little slumber.

To'evah, something detestable or an abomination. It names what is utterly repugnant to God, used in the law for idolatry and gross sin. It's striking that in verse 16 it describes arrogance, lying, and stirring up division among brothers, sins many people treat as minor.

christ: The chapter's list of what God hates stands in sharp contrast to the character of Jesus, who was humble rather than haughty, whose words were true, and who came to reconcile rather than sow discord (Ephesians 2:14-16). He was himself the victim of false witnesses at his trial (Mark 14:55-59), one of the very sins verse 19 names. The chapter's warning against becoming surety for another's debt meets a surprising reversal in the New Testament, where Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant: he took on the debt of others willingly, not rashly but by design. The link here is a striking contrast rather than a prediction, but it shows how the gospel both honors and exceeds the wisdom of Proverbs.

hard.q: Is it always wrong to guarantee a loan for someone, and does laziness always lead to poverty?
hard.a: These are proverbs, and they describe the usual pattern rather than an absolute law. The warning in verses 1 to 5 is against rash pledges, especially for a stranger, which could ruin a household; elsewhere the Bible commends generosity and lending to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7-8; Psalm 37:26). Many interpreters understand the book to be warning against guarantees you can't afford or that were made hastily, not forbidding all help to others. Likewise, verses 9 to 11 describe how laziness commonly leads to want. That doesn't mean every poor person is lazy. Proverbs itself recognizes poverty caused by injustice (13:23) and commands kindness to the poor. Reading the sluggard passage as an explanation for all poverty misreads the book and can harden a reader against people in real need.

questions: The ant works without a supervisor. What would change in your work if no one were checking on it?
Which of the seven things in verses 16 to 19 do you tend to treat as less serious than God does?
Verse 27 asks whether a man can embrace fire and not be burned. What fires do people try to hold while hoping to stay unharmed?
